One cell in this position can be solved with this technique. Find that cell, then write the digit it has to hold.
Tap the cell you think the technique solves.
Row %1$d, column %2$d is selected. Now pick its digit below.
The digit %1$d is picked. Now tap the cell it belongs in.
%1$d is not the solution of the selected cell, so nothing was written. Try another digit, or pick another cell.
The marked cells are where the pattern sits. What follows from it is yours to work out.

The examples for this technique could not be loaded.
This whole argument is about the digit %1$d. While it runs, every other candidate can be ignored.
The argument is made inside %1$s, outlined on the board. Only what happens in there counts.
The cells lit up now are the pattern itself. Look at what they have in common before reading on, that is what the technique is built on.
These two cells are linked: the digit fits in only these two places here, so if one of them does not hold it, the other one must.
Now follow both cases through. Whichever end of the link turns out to be true, the same conclusion is reached, which is what makes the next step safe.
In every one of those cases the crossed out candidates are impossible, so they can be rubbed out for good.
Nothing else survives the argument here, so this cell has to hold %1$d.
On the board: %1$s, and the candidates that matter there are %2$s.

A row, a column or a box that has only one empty cell left is missing exactly one digit, and that digit goes in that cell. You need no notes at all for this, just look at which digit the group has not used yet.
Look for a row, column or box with eight cells already filled. Glancing over the boxes for an almost full one after every few digits you write is the quickest way to catch them.

When one digit already sits in eight of the nine boxes, only one empty cell in the whole grid can still take it. Counting where the digit already is finds its last home, so no notes are needed here either.
Pick a digit and count how many boxes already show it. At eight, look at the box that is still missing it and find the one cell there the digit can still reach.
A cell has only one digit left when its row, its column and its box already show every other digit between them. That last digit has to go there. It is the most direct step in the game.
With notes: look for a cell with a single note left. Without notes: check cells that sit where a busy row and a busy column cross, they run out of options first.
Every digit appears exactly once in every box. If, inside one box, a digit fits in only one cell, it goes there, even when that cell still shows other notes. The digit is simply hidden behind them.
Take one digit and one box. Cross off every cell of the box that shares a row or a column with that digit somewhere outside. If a single cell survives, that is the placement.

The same idea along a row or a column: if a digit fits in only one cell of that line, it goes there. It is harder to see than in a box, because a line runs right across the grid instead of sitting in one block.
Walk one row or one column at a time and ask, for a single digit, which of its empty cells could still take it. Exactly one means you can place it.

Look at one digit inside one box. If every cell that could still take it sits on the same row or the same column, then the digit is somewhere on that line inside the box. Nowhere else on the line can hold it, so you can clear it from the rest of the line outside the box.
Inside a box, mark the cells that can still take one digit. If they all share a row or a column, follow that line out of the box and clear the digit there.

The same idea the other way round. If every cell of a row or column that could take a digit lies inside one box, then that box holds the digit on that line. So the digit can be cleared from the rest of the box.
Take one digit and one line. If all of its possible cells on that line fall inside a single box, clear the digit from the other cells of that box.

Two cells of the same row, column or box that both show exactly the same two notes will use up both of those digits between them, whichever way round they end up. No other cell of that group can take either digit.
Scan a group for two cells with exactly two notes each, and check whether the two notes are identical. Then clear those two digits from the rest of the group.
If two digits fit in only the same two cells of a group, those two cells are reserved for them. Every other note in those two cells can go, even though the pair was hidden behind them.
For each digit of a group, count the cells it could still go in. Two digits that share the same two cells are a hidden pair. Clean those two cells down to just those digits.

Three cells of one group whose notes together use only three different digits must hold exactly those three digits. They are used up, so no other cell of the group can take any of them. A cell that shows only two of the three still counts.
Look for three cells in one group whose notes together add up to just three different digits, then clear those digits from the rest of the group.
Three digits that fit in only the same three cells of a group own those cells. Every other note in those three cells can be cleared, and that is usually what opens the position up.
For each digit of a group, note the cells it could go in. Three digits whose cells cover only three positions are a hidden triple.

Take one digit and two rows in which it fits in only two cells each, with those cells standing in the same two columns. The four cells form a rectangle. Each row has to use one of the two columns, so between them they use both up, and the digit can be cleared from those columns in every other row.
Pick a digit and look for two rows where it has exactly two possible cells that line up in the same two columns. It works with rows and columns swapped as well.

Two rows in which a digit fits in only two cells each, and one cell of each sits in the same column. That column can hold the digit only once, so at least one of the two rows places it at its far end. One of the two far cells therefore holds the digit, and any cell that sees both of them loses it.
Find two rows where a digit has just two possible cells each, with one cell of each in the same column. Then look at the two far ends and at the cells that see both of them.

A row and a column in which a digit fits in only two cells each, with one end of the row and one end of the column landing in the same box. Those two near ends cannot both hold the digit, so one of the two far ends does. The cell where the far row cell and the far column cell cross loses the digit.
Look for a two cell row and a two cell column of the same digit whose near ends share a box. The elimination sits where the two far ends cross.

The X-Wing one size larger: three rows in which one digit fits only inside the same three columns. The three rows use those three columns up between them, so the digit can be cleared from those columns in every other row. A row that uses only two of the three still counts.
Pick a digit and look for three rows whose possible cells for it all fall inside a set of three columns. Rows and columns can swap roles.

Late in a puzzle you sometimes reach a position where every unsolved cell has exactly two notes, except one cell with three. If every cell had two, the puzzle could be finished in two different ways, which a proper puzzle never allows. The extra note is what prevents that, so it is the digit for that cell.
Check whether all remaining cells are down to two notes except a single cell with three. The odd digit out in that cell is the answer.

Three links of one digit joined end to end. A link is a row, column or box where the digit fits in only two cells, and two links join when one cell of each sees the other. Follow the chain: if the first end does not hold the digit, the far end has to. One of the two ends always does, so any cell that sees both of them loses the digit.
It is the skyscraper with one more link. Find three two cell links of one digit that chain together, then look at the cells that see both far ends.

Three cells with two notes each. The middle one, the pivot, shows two digits, and each of its two neighbours shares one of them and adds the same third digit. Whichever digit the pivot takes, one of the neighbours is pushed onto that third digit. So no cell that sees both neighbours can hold it.
Hunt for a two note cell that sees two other two note cells, sharing one digit with each of them, while those two share a third digit with each other. The elimination is where both neighbours look.

Four cells standing on two rows, two columns and only two boxes, holding nothing but the same two digits, could be filled in two ways, so the puzzle would have two solutions. A proper puzzle has one, so that cannot happen. When three corners are down to those two digits, the fourth must use one of its other notes, and both shared digits leave it.
Look for three corners of such a rectangle with the identical two notes, and a fourth corner holding those two plus extras. Clear the two shared digits from that corner.

The same rectangle, but this time two of the corners carry one and the same extra note. If neither used it, all four corners would be down to the two shared digits and the puzzle would have two solutions. So one of those two corners takes the extra digit, and every cell that sees both of them loses it.
Find a rectangle of two digits where two corners carry the same single extra note. Clear that extra digit from the cells both corners can see.

Like the XY-Wing, but the pivot carries three notes and both of its neighbours contain the third digit. One of the three cells has to take that digit, so a cell that sees all three of them cannot hold it. The victim has to see one cell more than in the XY-Wing, which is what makes it harder to use.
Find a three note pivot with two two note neighbours it sees, all three sharing one digit. The elimination must see the pivot and both neighbours.

Two far apart cells with the same two notes, say A and B, plus a row, column or box somewhere else where A fits in only two cells, one seeing the first cell and one seeing the second. Exactly one of those two holds A, and it pushes the cell it sees onto B. So one of the pair is B, and every cell seeing both of them loses B.
Look for two cells with identical two note sets, then check whether one of their digits has a two cell link joining them.

An X-Wing with a few extra cells for the digit on one of its rows, all sitting in one box. Those extras are the fin. Either the X-Wing holds, or the digit sits on a fin, and both cases put the digit inside that box. The usual eliminations therefore survive, but only inside the fin box.
Find an almost X-Wing where one row carries extra cells for the digit. If those extras all sit in a single box, you can still eliminate inside that box.

Four cells of one group using only four different digits between them take those four digits, so no other cell of the group can hold any of them. Cells showing only two or three of the four still count.
Look for four cells in one group whose notes together make up only four digits. It is easiest when at least two of them have just two notes.
Four digits that fit in only the same four cells of a group own those cells, so every other note in them can be cleared. It is rare, and often easier to spot as the naked subset it leaves behind.
For each digit of a group, list the cells it could go in. Four digits whose cells cover only four positions are the quad.

The same rectangle again, with extra notes in the two corners on one side. One of those two corners has to use one of its extras, otherwise the puzzle would have two solutions. The pair of corners therefore behaves like one cell holding all of those extras, and that stand in cell can form a naked pair, triple or quad with other cells of the group. The digits of that subset then leave the rest of the group.
Find the rectangle, take the extra notes of the two corners as one set, and look for cells in the same group that complete it into a naked pair, triple or quad.

The same rectangle, and one of the two shared digits fits in only the two corners of one side. That digit is certainly used by one of them. If the other corner took the second shared digit, all four corners would be down to the pair and the puzzle would have two solutions. So the second shared digit leaves both of those corners.
Find a rectangle of two digits and check whether one of them fits only in the two corners of its line. Then remove the other shared digit from those two corners.

Inside one box, every cell that could take a digit lies on one row and one column of that box, which leaves a clear rectangle of cells, and that is where the name comes from. The box holds the digit somewhere on that row or on that column. Add a line elsewhere where the digit fits in only two cells and points into the box, and the cell where the two arguments meet loses the digit.
Look for a box whose notes for one digit sit only on one row and one column, then find a line with exactly two cells for that digit pointing into it.

A swordfish with a few extra cells for the digit on its rows, all inside one box. As with the finned X-Wing, either the fish holds or the digit sits on a fin, so the eliminations still work, but only inside the fin box.
Find an almost swordfish where one line carries spare cells for the digit, and check whether those spares share a box with the cells you wanted to clear.

A finned swordfish with a corner missing: one of its three rows is down to a single cell inside the covering columns. The shape looks incomplete, which is what makes it hard to see, but the argument through the fin works exactly the same.
As the finned swordfish, except that one of the base lines has only one cell left inside the covering columns.
The fish one size larger again: four rows in which a digit fits only inside the same four columns. The four rows use those columns up, so the digit leaves those columns in every other row.
Pick a digit and look for four rows whose possible cells all fall inside a set of four columns. Anything smaller is a swordfish or an X-Wing.

Follow one digit through the groups where it fits in only two cells, painting those two ends in alternating colours. One whole colour is true and the other is false. If one colour turns up twice inside a single group it cannot be the true one, so the digit leaves every cell of that colour. And any cell that sees both colours loses the digit whichever colour wins.
Pick a digit, find the groups where it has only two places and colour the chain. Then look for one colour repeating inside a group, or for cells that see both colours.

Four cells that use exactly four digits between them. Three of those digits are restricted: every cell of the group that could take one of them sees the others, so each can be used only once here. Four cells cannot be filled from three digits, so one cell must take the fourth digit. Any cell that sees every group cell listing that digit loses it.
Look for four cells inside two groups whose notes total four digits, one of which appears in all the group cells a target cell can see.

A chain in a single digit, alternating between two kinds of link: strong ones, where at least one end must be true, and weak ones, where at most one end can be. Both ends of such a chain cannot be false at once, so any cell that sees both of them loses the digit. The skyscraper, the kite and the crane are its shortest forms.
Follow one digit through groups where it has only two places, then check the cells that see both ends of the chain.

A chain of cells that all have exactly two notes, each sharing a digit with the next. Entering a cell on one digit leaves it on the other, which is how the argument travels. If both ends can offer the same digit, every cell seeing both ends loses that digit. The XY-Wing is the three cell case.
Start at a two note cell and step to a neighbour that shares one of its digits, continuing until an end offers the digit you started with.

The general chain. It alternates strong and weak links like the others, but may switch digits inside a cell, so it can travel across digits freely. However the chain falls, one of its two ends is true, which rules candidates out of everything that sees both ends.
Build a chain that alternates strong and weak links across any digits, then check what both of its ends see together.

An almost locked set is a group of cells one digit short of being locked: four cells with five digits between them, for instance. Take two such sets sharing a digit that only one of the two can use. Then the other set is locked, whichever way it falls, so any second digit both sets share is certainly used inside one of them. Cells that see every place that digit could take in both sets lose it.
Find two almost locked sets, check that one shared digit can only be used by one of them, then clear the other shared digit from the cells both sets can see.

Look at the cells where a box and a line cross. If they list two more digits than they have cells, and you can find one more cell on the line and one more cell in the box that use only those digits and share none with each other, then every one of those digits is used exactly once inside the pattern. They are used up, so they leave the rest of the line and the rest of the box.

Take the two or three cells a box and a line share and count their digits. Two more digits than cells is the starting point, then hunt for one helper cell on the line and one in the box with no digit in common.

Simple colouring done across all digits at once, colouring single notes rather than whole cells. A cell with only two notes is a link as well, so the chain can hop from digit to digit inside a cell. One colour is entirely true and the other entirely false, and every contradiction that follows removes candidates: one colour twice in a cell, one colour twice for a digit in a group, or a note that sees both colours.

Colour a note, then colour everything it forces: the other note of a two note cell, and the other end of a group where the digit has two places. Then look for a colour appearing twice where it cannot.

An alternating chain in which a whole group of notes can act as a single link. When all the places for a digit inside one box sit on the same row or column, that group is true as soon as any of its cells holds the digit, so it behaves exactly like one note. Chains built this way reach conclusions no ordinary chain does.
Build a chain as usual, but allow a link to be all the places for a digit inside one box row or box column.

Three almost locked sets in a row, each pair joined by a digit only one of the two can use. The argument threads from the first set through the middle one to the last, so a digit both end sets list is certainly used by one of them. Cells that see every place that digit could take in both end sets lose it.
Join almost locked sets with digits that only one set of each pair can use, then clear the digit the two ends share from the cells that see all of its places.
